content: Delphinium is a genus comprising approximately 250 species of flowering plants, which can be annual, biennial, or perennial. These plants belong to the buttercup family, Ranunculaceae, and are native to regions across the Northern Hemisphere, as well as the high-altitude mountains of tropical Africa. The common name for these plants is larkspur, a term they share with the closely related genus Consolida. The leaves of Delphinium plants are deeply lobed, with 3 to 7 toothed, pointed segments. The primary flowering stem is upright and varies significantly in height depending on the species, ranging from as short as 10 cm in some alpine species to as tall as 2 meters in larger meadowland species. The stem is adorned with numerous flowers, which can appear in shades of purple, blue, red, yellow, or white. Each flower consists of five petals that are fused together to form a hollow structure with a spur at the end, a feature that inspired the plant's name. The seeds are small, shiny, and black. Delphinium plants bloom from late spring to late summer and are pollinated by butterflies and bumblebees. Despite their toxicity, certain Lepidoptera larvae, such as those of the Dot Moth and Small Angle Shades, use Delphinium species as a food source. Other historical names for the plant include lark's heel (as referenced by Shakespeare), lark's claw, and knight's spur. The scientific name Delphinium originates from Dioscorides and refers to the shape of the flower bud, which is thought to resemble a plump dolphin. The Forking Larkspur (Delphinium consolida) thrives in chalky loam soils and was once commonly found in cornfields, though it has become increasingly rare. Its flowers are typically purple, but a white variety also exists. Baker's larkspur (Delphinium bakeri) and Yellow larkspur (Delphinium luteum), both native to restricted areas of California, are critically endangered species. Many Delphinium species are cultivated as ornamental garden plants, with numerous cultivars selected for their dense and prominent flowers. However, all parts of the plant contain the alkaloid delphinine, making them highly toxic. Ingestion can cause vomiting and, in larger quantities, death. Despite this, small amounts of plant extracts have been used in herbal medicine. Gerard's herbal text mentions that consuming larkspur seeds was believed to counteract scorpion stings and immobilize other poisonous animals when covered with the herb, though Gerard himself expressed skepticism about these claims. Grieve's herbal notes that the seeds can be used to combat parasites, particularly lice and their nits in hair. Additionally, a tincture derived from the plant has been used to treat asthma and dropsy. The juice of the flowers, when mixed with alum, produces a blue ink. Historically, the plant was associated with Saint Odile and was used in folk medicine to treat eye diseases. It was also one of the herbs used during the feast of St. John, believed to protect against lightning. In Transylvania, larkspur was used to ward off witches from stables, likely due to its blue color. Larkspur, particularly tall larkspur, is a significant cause of cattle poisoning on rangelands in the western United States. The plant is more prevalent in high-elevation areas, and ranchers often delay moving cattle to such ranges until late summer, when the plant's toxicity diminishes.
